q-161326.name: Question 1
q-161326.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2}y,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-\sqrt{2}x-y$ for $-1\le x\le 0$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
q-161326.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{2}x-y)=-\sqrt{2},
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{2}x-y)=-1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}y\cdot 2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,2\sqrt{2}y\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=2y, where the surface S is defined by z=−2x−y for −1≤x≤0 and 0≤y≤2. This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. ∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∫−10∫02AAAAAAAdydx

What is the missing expression?

a
42y
b
−22y
c
2y
d
−42y2
e
22y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=g(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f(x,y,z) over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

For the partial derivatives, we have

∂z∂x=∂∂x(−2x−y)=−2, and ∂z∂y=∂∂y(−2x−y)=−1.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(−2)2+(−1)2dA=∬D2y⋅2dA=∫−10∫0222ydydx.

q-161106.name: Question 2
q-161106.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=2xy,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
q-161106.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(2x)}^{2}+{(2y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2xy\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,2xy\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161351.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(24xy+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=3x-4y$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
q-161351.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x-4y)=3,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x-4y)=-4.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(24xy+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(24xy+(3x-4y)^{2})\sqrt{1+{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{26}{∬}_{D}\,(24xy+9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}-24xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{26}{∬}_{D}\,(9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{1}^{2}{[9{x}^{2}y+\frac{16}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{1}^{2}(9{x}^{2}+\frac{16}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{26}{[3{x}^{3}+\frac{16}{3}x]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\sqrt{26}(24+\frac{32}{3}-3-\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{79}{3}\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}
$$

q-161342.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-161342.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x)=0.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(0)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}-2x(0-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=4x+\sqrt{3}y$ and whose domain is the circle of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
q-161338.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+\sqrt{3}y)=4,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+\sqrt{3}y)=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{1+{4}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{20}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}(1-{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(r-{r}^{3})\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{5}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120383/assets/0b1b263baf01b692a0344388207c12d3c4dac0f49d11cd4bfa744f2841df2c6b.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x-\sqrt{2}y$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O$ in the fourth quadrant, as shown above.
q-161316.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot r\text{ }\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}2r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta [{r}^{2}]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\,\text{d}r \\  & =9[-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =9\cdot (-1-1) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$
